title: Transfer Functions and Realisations
intro: The state equations look inside the system; the transfer function $G(s)$ looks only at what goes in and what comes out. This page derives $G(s) = C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D$, shows where its poles and zeros come from, and runs the other way: building a state-space model from a given $G(s)$, which can be done in many ways.

blocks.text: From the state equations to G(s)

The Laplace transform turns derivatives into multiplication by $s$ (see The Laplace Transform (#/math/laplace-transform) and Solving Differential Equations (#/math/laplace-transform/differential-equations)). A transfer function relates the transformed input to the transformed output when the system starts at rest, so we take $x(0) = 0$. Transform $x' = Ax + Bu$ and $y = Cx + Du$, with $X(s)$, $U(s)$, $Y(s)$ for the transforms:

blocks.tex: sX(s) = AX(s) + BU(s), \qquad Y(s) = CX(s) + DU(s)

blocks.text: Collect the $X$ terms: $(sI - A)X(s) = BU(s)$. Here $sI$, not $s$ alone, because $A$ is a matrix and $s$ a number. Multiply by the inverse of $sI - A$ (it exists for every $s$ that is not an eigenvalue of $A$), and put the result into the output equation:

blocks.tex: X(s) = (sI - A)^{-1}BU(s), \qquad G(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{U(s)} = C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D

blocks.text: This is the transfer function. For one input and one output it is a ratio of polynomials in $s$. The inverse transform of $G(s)$ is the impulse response $Ce^{At}B$ found on the page Solving the State Equations (#/math/state-space/solving): the same fact, seen through the Laplace transform of $e^{At}$.
Worked: the mass and the circuit
For the light mass, $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -4 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (0, 1)^{\top}$, $C = (1, 0)$, $D = 0$:

blocks.tex: sI - A = \begin{pmatrix} s & -1 \\ 4 & s + 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad (sI - A)^{-1} = \frac{1}{s^2 + s + 4}\begin{pmatrix} s + 1 & 1 \\ -4 & s \end{pmatrix}

blocks.text: The determinant is $s(s + 1) - (-1)(4) = s^2 + s + 4$. The inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix swaps the diagonal, negates the off-diagonal and divides by the determinant. Multiply by $B$: the column $(0, 1)$ picks the second column of the inverse, $\frac{1}{s^2 + s + 4}(1, s)$. Then $C = (1, 0)$ picks the first entry, so

which is just the Laplace transform of $\ddot p + \dot p + 4p = u$ read as output over input. For the RLC circuit, $sI - A = \begin{pmatrix} s & -2 \\ 1 & s + 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $s(s + 2) + 2 = s^2 + 2s + 2$, and the inverse has second column $\frac{1}{s^2 + 2s + 2}(2, s)$ (the second column of $\mathrm{adj}$: the entries $-(-2) = 2$ and $s$). With $B = (0, 1)$ and $C = (1, 0)$ we read off the first entry: $G(s) = 2/(s^2 + 2s + 2)$. The steady-state gain is $G(0) = 2/2 = 1$: a constant voltage is passed through unchanged, which matches the resting point $(1, 0)$ on the previous page.
Poles are eigenvalues

Every entry of the inverse of a matrix is a cofactor divided by the determinant: $(sI - A)^{-1} = \mathrm{adj}(sI - A)/\det(sI - A)$. The numerator is a matrix of polynomials of degree less than $n$ and the denominator is the characteristic polynomial of $A$. So

The denominator has degree $n$, and its roots are the eigenvalues of $A$. So the poles of $G(s)$ are among the eigenvalues. 'Among' is deliberate: if the numerator is also zero at an eigenvalue, the factor cancels and that eigenvalue is not a pole of $G$. The system still has the mode $e^{\lambda t}$, but it never shows up in the relation from input to output. Which is exactly the situation of hidden modes.
Hidden modes: a preview
Take $A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (1, 0)^{\top}$, $C = (1, 1)$. The matrix is diagonal, so $(sI - A)^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}\left(\frac{1}{s+1},\ \frac{1}{s+2}\right)$, and

The system has two eigenvalues, $-1$ and $-2$, but $G(s)$ has only one pole. The input $B = (1, 0)$ pushes only the first state; the second never moves, so the mode $e^{-2t}$ is never excited. The viewer prints the unreduced form $(s + 2)/(s^2 + 3s + 2)$, with a pole and a zero both at $-2$ sitting on top of each other. The other preset has $B = (1, 1)$, $C = (1, 0)$: the input excites both states, but the output reads only the first, so again $G = 1/(s + 1)$. The names of the two situations, not controllable and not observable, and the rank tests for them are on the page Controllability and Observability (#/math/state-space/controllability-observability).

blocks.text: The System is 'hidden mode: the input misses one', Input unit step, $x(0) = 0$. In the time plot the amber $x_2$ stays on zero for ever; the blue $x_1$ and the thick red $y$ (the same here, since $y = x_1 + x_2$) rise to $1$. The readout says 'Not controllable, observable' and ends 'At t = 5 s: x = (0.99, 0.00), y = 0.993', which is $1 - e^{-5}$, the step response of $1/(s + 1)$. In the pole-zero plot bottom right there are two poles at $-1$ and $-2$ and a zero at $-2$ on top of the second pole. Step 7 of the walk-through (Next step ▶) says the pole 'cancels against a zero and G looks first order'. Now switch System to 'hidden mode: the output misses one': $x_2$ now rises to $0.5$ but $y$ is the same curve as before.
Zeros

The poles come from $A$ alone. The zeros, the roots of the numerator, depend on $B$ and $C$ as well, so choosing what to measure moves them. Keep the mass but measure position plus velocity, $C = (1, 1)$: the row $(1, 1)$ times the column $\frac{1}{s^2 + s + 4}(1, s)$ gives $(1 + s)/(s^2 + s + 4)$. The poles are the same $-0.5 \pm 1.936j$, but there is now a zero at $s = -1$. A zero is a value of $s$ at which the system blocks an input of the form $e^{st}$. Here the numerator $s + 1$ means the output responds to the rate of change of the input as well as to its size. See the page Pole Positions and the Time Signal (#/math/laplace-transform/poles-and-time) for how poles and zeros shape a response.
From G(s) back to state space
Given a transfer function, can you find $(A, B, C, D)$? Yes, in many ways. Take the strictly proper second-order case

First method. Introduce an intermediate signal $\xi$ with $\xi'' + a_1\xi' + a_0\xi = u$, so that $\Xi(s) = U(s)/(s^2 + a_1s + a_0)$, and build the output as $y = b_1\xi' + b_0\xi$, whose transform is $(b_1s + b_0)\Xi$, which is $G(s)U(s)$. Take $x_1 = \xi$ and $x_2 = \xi'$: the same recipe as the page States and the State Equations (#/math/state-space/state-equations) gives $x_1' = x_2$, $x_2' = -a_0x_1 - a_1x_2 + u$, and the output reads $y = b_0x_1 + b_1x_2$:

This is the controllable canonical form, also called the companion form. All the coefficients of the denominator are in the last row of $A$, all those of the numerator in $C$. Second method: transpose everything. Take $A^{\top}$, put $C^{\top}$ in the place of $B$ and $B^{\top}$ in the place of $C$ (the transfer function of a single-input single-output system does not change when you transpose it, since a $1 \times 1$ number equals its own transpose):

This is the observable canonical form. Worked example: $G(s) = \dfrac{2s + 3}{s^2 + 3s + 2}$, so $a_1 = 3$, $a_0 = 2$, $b_1 = 2$, $b_0 = 3$. Controllable form: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (0, 1)^{\top}$, $C = (3, 2)$. Check by computing $C(sI - A)^{-1}B$: with $A$ as the heavy mass, $(sI - A)^{-1}B = \frac{1}{s^2 + 3s + 2}(1, s)$ from the previous computation, and $C = (3, 2)$ gives $(3 + 2s)/(s^2 + 3s + 2)$. Correct. Observable form: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 1 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (3, 2)^{\top}$, $C = (0, 1)$. Check: $sI - A = \begin{pmatrix} s & 2 \\ -1 & s + 3 \end{pmatrix}$, its inverse is $\frac{1}{s^2 + 3s + 2}\begin{pmatrix} s + 3 & -2 \\ 1 & s \end{pmatrix}$, and $C$ picks the second row $(1, s)$; times $B = (3, 2)$ gives $3 + 2s$. Correct again.

These two models are different matrices describing the same input-output behaviour. In general, a change of state $z = Tx$ (the page States and the State Equations (#/math/state-space/state-equations)) gives $(TAT^{-1}, TB, CT^{-1})$, and the transfer function does not change: $CT^{-1}(sI - TAT^{-1})^{-1}TB = CT^{-1}\,T(sI - A)^{-1}T^{-1}\,TB = C(sI - A)^{-1}B$, because $sI - TAT^{-1} = T(sI - A)T^{-1}$. And there are realisations of different sizes, too: the hidden-mode presets realise $1/(s + 1)$ with two states, where one state is enough. A realisation with the fewest possible states is called minimal. Every $G(s)$ has one, and a given realisation is minimal exactly when no mode is hidden, that is, when it is both controllable and observable, as the page Controllability and Observability (#/math/state-space/controllability-observability) explains.
Frequency response and steady-state gain

Put $s = j\omega$ in $G(s)$ and you get the frequency response (see The Imaginary Axis and Frequency Response (#/math/laplace-transform/imaginary-axis)): a stable system driven by $\cos\omega t$ ends up oscillating at the same frequency, scaled by $|G(j\omega)|$ and shifted by the phase of $G(j\omega)$. For the light mass at $\omega = 2$, the natural frequency, $G(2j) = 1/(-4 + 2j + 4) = 1/(2j) = -0.5j$: size $0.5$ and phase $-90^\circ$. At $\omega = 0$ we get the steady-state gain, which in state-space terms is

(Put $s = 0$ in $C(sI - A)^{-1}B$: $(0 - A)^{-1} = -A^{-1}$.) This is the same $-CA^{-1}B$ as the output at the resting point on the page Solving the State Equations (#/math/state-space/solving): mass $0.25$, RLC $1$, two tanks $2$. When $A$ is singular, $G(0)$ is infinite: that is a pole at $s = 0$, which is the DC motor.

blocks.text: The System is the DC motor, Input unit step. The readout gives $G(s) = (2)/(s^2 + 2s)$: the denominator is $s(s + 2)$, with poles $0$ and $-2$ marked in the pole-zero plot bottom right, one of them on the boundary of the shaded right half. There is no zero (the numerator is the constant 2), and there is no red +, because there is no resting point: $G(0)$ would be $2/0$. In the time plot the thick red $y$ (the angle) ends at 7.5 at $t = 8$ s, still climbing. The pole at $0$ is an integrator: the angle is the running sum of the speed.
Practice

blocks.title: Transfer function of the tanks
blocks.text: Find $G(s)$ for the two tanks, $A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (1, 0)^{\top}$, $C = (0, 1)$, and the steady-state gain.
solution: $sI - A = \begin{pmatrix} s + 1 & 0 \\ -1 & s + 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $(s + 1)(s + 0.5) = s^2 + 1.5s + 0.5$. Its inverse is $\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+0.5)}\begin{pmatrix} s + 0.5 & 0 \\ 1 & s + 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
$B = (1, 0)$ picks the first column, $(s + 0.5,\ 1)$ over the determinant; $C = (0, 1)$ picks the second entry, $1$. So $G(s) = 1/(s^2 + 1.5s + 0.5)$.
$G(0) = 1/0.5 = 2$, the level of tank 2 for a unit inflow, as found by the resting point $(1, 2)$.

blocks.title: Both canonical forms
blocks.text: Write the controllable and the observable canonical forms for $G(s) = \dfrac{s + 1}{s^2 + 2s + 5}$ and find its poles and zero.
solution: The poles are the roots of $s^2 + 2s + 5$: $s = -1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 5} = -1 \pm 2j$. The zero is $s = -1$. No cancellation, since $-1$ is not a pole.
blocks.answer: Controllable: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -5 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (0,1)^{\top}$, $C = (1,1)$. Observable: transposed arrangement above. Poles $-1 \pm 2j$, zero $-1$.

blocks.title: A hidden pole
blocks.text: For $A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (1, 1)^{\top}$, $C = (1, 0)$, find $G(s)$ and say what the state $x_2$ does when $u = 1$.
solution: Diagonal $A$ again, so $(sI - A)^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(1/(s+1),\ 1/(s+2))$. Then $C(sI - A)^{-1}B$ picks the first diagonal entry times $B_1 = 1$: $G(s) = 1/(s + 1)$.

The second state obeys $x_2' = -2x_2 + u$, which with $u = 1$ goes to $0.5$. It does move, but the output never sees it: $y = x_1$ obeys $x_1' = -x_1 + u$ by itself. This is the preset 'hidden mode: the output misses one', and the readout prints 'x = (0.99, 0.50), y = 0.993' at $t = 5$ s.

blocks.title: Frequency response of the circuit
blocks.text: For the RLC circuit, $G(s) = 2/(s^2 + 2s + 2)$. Find $|G(j\omega)|$ and the phase at $\omega = 1$.
solution: Put $s = j$: $s^2 = -1$, so the denominator is $-1 + 2j + 2 = 1 + 2j$ and $G(j) = 2/(1 + 2j)$.
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate: $2(1 - 2j)/(1 + 4) = 0.4 - 0.8j$.

The size is $\sqrt{0.16 + 0.64} = 0.894$, and the phase is $\arctan(-0.8/0.4) = -63.4^\circ$ (the output lags the input). The gain is below the DC gain $1$ because the circuit passes slow signals better than fast ones.

blocks.text: Sources and further reading

items: Katsuhiko Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, 5th edition (Prentice Hall, 2010). Chapter 9 treats the transfer function and state space together, including canonical forms.
Chi-Tsong Chen, Linear System Theory and Design, 4th edition (Oxford University Press, 2013). Chapter 4 covers state-space solutions and realisations.

Gene F. Franklin, J. David Powell and Abbas Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems, 7th edition (Pearson, 2015). Chapter 7 covers state-space models and the canonical forms used for design.

Karl Johan Åström and Richard M. Murray, Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers, 2nd edition (Princeton University Press, 2021). Its chapter on transfer functions shows how a transfer function follows from the state equations.
